title: How machine learning can tackle lead pipe challenges
excerpt: A new machine learning tool developed through the Centre for Resilience in Environment, Water and Waste (CREWW) could help water companies identify properties most likely to be connected to lead service pipes.
content_html:
A new machine learning tool developed through the Centre for Resilience in Environment, Water and Waste (CREWW) could help water companies identify properties most likely to be connected to lead service pipes.

The newly published study, "The Effectiveness of Different Ground Truths at Detecting Lead Service Pipes Using Machine Learning," demonstrates how advanced data analytics can be used to predict the presence of lead pipes, and what data is needed for this to be effective, where historic records are incomplete or unavailable. The paper is published in the Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management.

By combining operational knowledge with academic research, the project is helping to develop smarter ways of locating lead pipes across the water network where historic records may be incomplete or unavailable.

Lead pipes remain one of the water sector's longstanding challenges. While no longer installed, legacy lead piping can still be found in both public and private water supply systems, making their identification and replacement an ongoing priority for water companies. The new tool uses machine learning techniques to analyze available data sets and predict where lead communication and supply pipes are most likely to exist.

By helping target investigations and replacement programs more effectively, the approach could reduce costs, improve efficiency and accelerate progress toward reducing lead piping.

The publication is the latest example of how CREWW—a collaboration between the University of Exeter and South West Water—is bringing together academic expertise and operational experience to develop practical solutions to challenges facing the water sector, translating research into innovations that can deliver benefits for customers, communities and the environment.

Matt Hayslep, postdoctoral research fellow from the University of Exeter, said, "Removing lead pipes is important from an industry, health and environment point of view, and it is very exciting that our research is helping South West Water to do this more effectively. There have been a lot of interesting machine learning and data challenges, which we continue to work hard to overcome as we improve the tool. Our success so far demonstrates the value of industrial partnerships with the University of Exeter."

Jason Harvey, networks transformation and innovation manager at South West Water, said, "Improving our understanding of where lead pipes are located is an important part of our long-term ambition to become lead-free by 2050. This project demonstrates how collaboration through CREWW can help turn research into practical tools that support operational decision-making. By using machine learning and advanced analytics, we're developing new ways to target investigations more effectively and improve how we manage our network."

More information

Matthew Hayslep et al., Effectiveness of Different Ground Truths at Detecting Lead Service Pipes Using Machine Learning, Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management (2027). DOI: 10.1061/jwrmd5.wreng-7717
